content.statement: When you run a program such as ls from a shell, it runs as a child process of that shell.

remember: Every command you start from a shell is a child process with its own PID, and the shell is its parent.

content.prompt: You run ./server & in a terminal. What does the & do?

options.text: Starts the server in the background, so the prompt returns at once
Runs the server only if the previous command succeeded
Runs the server at a lower CPU priority
Runs the server with root rights

remember: A trailing & runs a command in the background; it is still the shell's child and can die when you log out.

content.prompt: Both imports always succeed, but the report is sometimes built from incomplete data. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Replace it with a plain wait

remember: wait $! waits only for the last background job; a plain wait waits for all of the shell's children.

content.prompt: You type ls in bash and press Enter. Put the steps in order.

steps.text: ls runs, prints the listing and exits with status 0
The shell prints the next prompt
bash calls fork(), creating a copy of itself
The shell's wait() returns the child's exit status
The child calls exec(), replacing its program with ls

remember: Unix starts a program with fork, then exec in the child; the parent's wait collects the exit status.

content.prompt: ps shows a worker in state Z, marked <defunct>. Its parent is still running. What removes the zombie?

options.text: Sending SIGKILL to the zombie's PID
Sending SIGCONT so it can finish exiting
Nothing: the kernel frees it when PIDs run low
The parent calling wait() on it, or the parent exiting

remember: A zombie has already exited; it stays in the process table until its parent reaps it with wait(), or until init adopts and reaps it.

content.statement: Threads of the same process share its heap memory, so one thread can read objects another thread created.

remember: Threads share their process's memory; separate processes do not, unless they set up shared memory explicitly.

content.prompt: In Java, two threads each run counter++ one million times on a shared int field, with no lock. What is the typical result?

options.text: Often below 2,000,000, and different on each run
Exactly 1,000,000, because the threads overwrite each other
Above 2,000,000, because some increments run twice

remember: counter++ is a read, an add and a write; without a lock two threads interleave them and lose updates.

content.prompt: What does this print?
content.code:
import threading
import multiprocessing as mp

items = []

def work():
    items.append("x")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    t = threading.Thread(target=work)
    t.start()
    t.join()
    p = mp.Process(target=work)
    p.start()
    p.join()
    print(len(items))

remember: A thread appends to the list its process shares; a child process changes only its own copy of memory.

content.prompt: Under load, two customers sometimes both buy the last lamp and the stock drops to -1. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Take the lock before the check, so check and update run together

remember: Check-then-act must run under one lock; a check made before taking the lock can be stale by the time you act.

content.statement: In C, memory allocated with malloc is freed automatically when the function that called malloc returns.

remember: A stack frame disappears when its function returns, but heap memory from malloc lives until free is called.

content.prompt: A recursive function with a missing base case crashes after thousands of nested calls. Which memory ran out?

options.text: The heap, because each call allocates its arguments there
The CPU cache, because each call is stored there
The stack, because each call adds a frame until the limit is hit
Swap space, because old frames are written to disk

remember: Every call pushes a frame onto a fixed-size stack, so unbounded recursion overflows it.

content.prompt: Inside a C function, three of these live on the stack. Which one lives on the heap?

items.text: The return address saved by the call

remember: Locals and return addresses live in the call's stack frame; malloc hands out heap memory that outlives the call.

content.prompt: After fork(), the child sets the global x to 99. Both processes then print &x and x: the addresses match, but the parent prints 0 and the child 99. Why?

options.text: The parent read x before the child's write reached memory
Each process has its own virtual address space, mapped to different physical memory
printf prints an offset in the program file, not a memory address
The kernel blocks writes to globals in the child until the parent exits

remember: Addresses a program sees are virtual: the same address in two processes can map to different physical memory.

content.prompt: A program reads an address whose page is on disk, not in RAM. Put the steps in order.

steps.text: The kernel reads the page from disk into a free frame
The CPU retries the instruction, which now succeeds
The MMU finds no valid mapping and raises a page fault
The program's load instruction uses the virtual address
The kernel updates the page table to point at that frame

remember: A page fault traps into the kernel, which loads the page, fixes the page table and lets the instruction run again.

content.statement: On a typical Linux filesystem such as ext4, Report.txt and report.txt in the same directory are the same file.

remember: Linux file names are case-sensitive: Report.txt and report.txt are two different files.

content.prompt: The current directory is /home/ana/project. Which path points to /home/ana/notes.txt?

remember: . is the current directory and .. its parent; only a path that starts with / starts at the root.

content.prompt: What does ls print?
content.code:
mkdir demo
cd demo
touch .env app.js notes.txt
ls

remember: Names that start with a dot are hidden from ls; ls -a shows them.

content.prompt: Match each directory with what it holds on a typical Linux system.

right.text: Scratch files any user may write, not kept for long
System-wide configuration files
Virtual files the kernel generates about processes
Log files written by services

remember: /etc holds configuration, /var/log logs, /tmp temporary files, and /proc is a virtual view of the processes.

content.prompt: data.txt has a hard link hard.txt and a symbolic link soft.txt. After rm data.txt, three of these commands still succeed. Which one fails?

remember: A hard link is another name for the same inode, so the data survives rm; a symlink stores only a path, which now points nowhere.

content.statement: After chmod 644 file.txt, the owner can read and write the file, and everyone else can only read it.

remember: Each octal digit is owner, group, others; 4 is read, 2 write and 1 execute, so 644 is rw-r--r--.

content.prompt: ls -l shows -rwxr-x--- for deploy.sh. What may members of the file's group do?

options.text: Read and execute it, but not change it
Nothing: the group has no rights

remember: After the file type come three triplets for owner, group and others; r-x means read and execute, no write.

content.prompt: What does this print?
content.code:
touch run.sh
chmod 600 run.sh
chmod u+x,go+r run.sh
stat -c '%a' run.sh

remember: Symbolic chmod adds or removes bits on top of the current mode: 600 plus u+x and go+r gives 744.

content.prompt: Fill the blank so new files get mode 640 and new directories 750.

remember: umask lists the bits to remove from 666 for files and 777 for directories, so 027 gives 640 and 750.

content.prompt: Match each ls -l mode with what it means.

right.text: New files inside get the directory's group
Others can open files whose names they know, but cannot list it
Runs with the rights of the file's owner, not of the caller
Anyone can create files, but users can delete only their own

remember: s in the owner triplet is setuid, s in a directory's group triplet is setgid, and t is the sticky bit, as on /tmp.

content.statement: The root account has user ID 0.

remember: The kernel treats UID 0 as the superuser; root is just the usual name for that account.

content.prompt: Why do admins run sudo apt update instead of working in a root shell all day?

options.text: Commands run through sudo are faster than in a root shell
root cannot install packages; only sudo can
Only that one command gets root rights, and sudo logs who ran it
sudo needs no password and no permission setup

remember: sudo grants root rights one command at a time and logs it, so ordinary work cannot break the system by accident.

content.prompt: The script prints "Permission denied" and /etc/hosts stays unchanged, although the user may use sudo. Find the bug.
content.code:
#!/bin/bash
# add local host names for development
sudo mkdir -p /etc/myapp
sudo cp app.conf /etc/myapp/
sudo echo "127.0.0.1 api.local" >> /etc/hosts
echo "done"

fixes.text: Run sudo -E echo so the environment is kept
Pipe the echo into sudo tee -a /etc/hosts instead

remember: Your own shell opens the >> file before sudo starts; write root-owned files with sudo tee or sudo sh -c.

content.prompt: Match each file with what it stores.

right.text: Groups and their members
Who may run which commands as root
Password hashes, hidden from normal users
Accounts with their UID, home directory and shell

remember: /etc/passwd lists accounts, /etc/shadow holds password hashes, /etc/group lists groups, and /etc/sudoers says who may use sudo.

content.prompt: Fill the blank to add ana to the docker group without removing her from her other groups.

remember: usermod -aG appends a group; -G alone replaces all supplementary groups, and the change applies at the next login.

content.statement: In bash, command > out.txt adds the output to the end of out.txt and keeps what was already there.

remember: > empties the file before writing; >> appends to it.

content.prompt: Which command saves only the error messages of make into errors.log?

remember: File descriptor 1 is stdout and 2 is stderr, so 2> redirects only the errors.

content.prompt: Fill the blank so the build output shows in the terminal and is also saved to build.log.

remember: tee copies its input both to a file and to stdout, so you can watch output and keep it.

content.prompt: What appears in the terminal?

remember: Redirections run left to right: 2>&1 > file points stderr at the old stdout, then moves only stdout to the file.

content.prompt: The script lists the files with errors, but always reports "0 files with errors" and exits 0. Find the bug.
content.code:
#!/bin/bash
failed=0
grep -l ERROR logs/*.log | while read -r file; do
  echo "errors in $file"
  failed=$((failed + 1))
done
echo "$failed files with errors"
if [ "$failed" -gt 0 ]; then exit 1; fi

fixes.text: Declare failed with export so the loop can update it
Drop the pipe and end the loop with done < <(grep -l ERROR logs/*.log)

remember: Each part of a bash pipeline runs in a subshell, so variables set in a piped while loop are lost; use process substitution.

content.statement: grep -v ERROR app.log prints only the lines that do not contain ERROR.

remember: grep -v inverts the match and prints the lines that do not match.

content.prompt: Which command prints how many lines of app.log contain ERROR?

remember: grep -c counts the matching lines; grep ... | wc -l gives the same number.

content.prompt: What does this print?
content.code:
cat > visits.txt <<'EOF'
ana
ben
ana
ana
EOF
uniq visits.txt | wc -l

remember: uniq removes only adjacent duplicates, so sort first: sort | uniq.

content.prompt: Order the stages of a pipeline that prints the 3 IP addresses with the most requests in access.log, where the IP is the first field.

steps.text: sort -rn
awk '{print $1}' access.log
head -3
uniq -c
sort

remember: Extract the field, sort so duplicates touch, count them with uniq -c, sort by count with sort -rn, then take the top with head.

content.prompt: Some nights the job fails with "find: paths must precede expression"; on others it removes only old files named app.log. Find the bug.

#!/bin/bash
# nightly cleanup of old logs
set -euo pipefail
cd /srv/app/logs
find . -type f -name *.log -mtime +7 -delete

remember: Quote find patterns such as '*.log'; unquoted, the shell first expands them to matching names in the current directory.

content.statement: If API_KEY is not set yet, running API_KEY=abc123 without export makes it visible to programs started later from that shell.

remember: A plain assignment creates a shell variable; only export puts it into the environment that child processes get.

content.prompt: What does PORT=4000 npm start do?

options.text: Sets PORT for the rest of the shell session, then runs npm start
Saves PORT=4000 permanently in the user's profile
Passes 4000 to npm start as a command-line argument
Runs npm start with PORT=4000 in its environment only

remember: VAR=value command sets the variable only in that command's environment; the shell itself is unchanged.

content.prompt: Three of these print your home directory. Which one does not?

remember: Single quotes stop expansion, so '$HOME' prints literally; double quotes expand it and still protect spaces.

content.prompt: Fill the blank so the script uses 8080 whenever PORT is unset or empty.

remember: ${VAR:-default} uses the default when VAR is unset or empty; ${VAR-default} only when it is unset.

content.prompt: What does this print?
content.code:
A=1
export A
A=2
B=3 bash -c 'echo "child: $A $B"'
echo "parent: $A [$B]"

remember: export marks the name, so later assignments are exported too; a VAR=value prefix sets the variable for that one command only.

content.statement: A program can install a handler for SIGKILL to save its work before it stops.

remember: SIGKILL and SIGSTOP cannot be caught or ignored; send SIGTERM to give a program a chance to clean up.

content.prompt: Which signal does kill 1234 send when no signal is named?

remember: kill sends SIGTERM by default, a polite request to stop that the program can handle.

content.prompt: Match each action with the signal the program receives.

right.text: SIGHUP
SIGKILL
SIGINT
SIGTSTP

remember: Ctrl+C sends SIGINT, Ctrl+Z SIGTSTP, a closed terminal SIGHUP, and kill -9 SIGKILL.

content.prompt: docker stop hits an app that handles SIGTERM but then hangs while closing its database connection. Put what happens in order.

steps.text: The grace period runs out
The app's handler stops accepting new requests
Docker sends SIGKILL and the process ends at once
Docker sends SIGTERM to the container's main process
The app hangs waiting for the database to close

remember: Stopping a service sends SIGTERM, waits a grace period, then sends SIGKILL, so shutdown handlers must finish in time.

content.prompt: On docker stop, the server's SIGTERM handler never runs and every stop takes the full timeout. Find the bug.
content.code:
#!/bin/sh
# entrypoint.sh, the container's ENTRYPOINT
set -e
echo "running migrations"
node migrate.js
echo "starting server"

fixes.text: Add trap '' TERM at the top of the script
Start the server in the background: node server.js &
Start the server with exec node server.js

content.statement: By convention, a program that exits with status 0 succeeded.

remember: Exit status 0 means success and 1 to 255 mean failure; $? holds the status of the last command.

content.prompt: A deploy script runs npm test && ./deploy.sh. When does ./deploy.sh run?

options.text: Only when npm test exits with status 0
Only when npm test exits with a non-zero status
At the same time as npm test

remember: a && b runs b only if a succeeded; a || b runs b only if a failed.

content.prompt: In a directory without a file named missing.txt, three of these commands exit with status 0. Which one does not?

remember: A command that cannot do its job, like cat on a missing file, exits with a non-zero status.

content.prompt: The script deploys even when the tests fail. Find the bug.
content.code:
#!/bin/bash
npm test
status=$?
echo "tests finished with status $status"
if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then
  echo "tests failed, not deploying"
  exit 1
fi
./deploy.sh

remember: $? changes after every command, so save it right away and test the saved variable.

options.text: Nothing: set -e stops the script at false

remember: set -e is ignored inside anything tested by ||, &&, if or while, including the whole body of a function called there.

content.statement: systemctl enable nginx starts nginx right away.

remember: enable makes a service start at boot; start runs it now, and enable --now does both.

content.prompt: app.service keeps failing. Which command follows its log live?

remember: systemd collects service output in the journal; journalctl -u <unit> -f follows one unit's log.

steps.text: Run systemctl enable --now app
Check systemctl status app
Copy app.service to /etc/systemd/system/
Run systemctl daemon-reload

remember: After adding or editing a unit file, run systemctl daemon-reload before starting or enabling it.

content.prompt: Match each unit file line with what it does.

right.text: If both start, start this unit after PostgreSQL
Lets systemctl enable start the unit at boot
The account the service process runs as
The command systemd runs to start the service

content.prompt: app.service has Restart=on-failure. Three of these make systemd start it again. Which one does not?

items.text: Someone runs kill -9 on the app's PID
The app finishes and exits with status 0
The app crashes with a segmentation fault

remember: Restart=on-failure restarts after a non-zero exit or an unclean signal such as SIGKILL or SIGSEGV, but not after exit status 0.
